meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Mixes conceptual understanding, code reading, debugging, and output prediction to build software engineering skills

back.content:
Output:
2
1
2.5

Explanation:
• x / y = 5 / 2 → INTEGER division truncates decimal → 2 (not 2.5!)
• x % y = 5 % 2 → remainder after dividing → 1
• (double) x / y → cast x to 2.5 first, THEN divide → 2.5

🐛 Common Bug: Expecting 5/2 = 2.5 but getting 2. Fix: cast to double first.
💡 Modulo (%) is useful: check even/odd (n%2==0), check divisibility (n%10==0 means ends in 0)

front.content:
🔍 PREDICT THE OUTPUT — Pre vs Post Increment:

int i = 5;
System.out.println(i++);  // Line A
System.out.println(++i);  // Line B
System.out.println(i);    // Line C

back.content:
Output:
5   ← Line A: i++ is POST-increment. Returns 5, THEN i becomes 6.
7   ← Line B: ++i is PRE-increment. i becomes 7, THEN returns 7.
7   ← Line C: i is still 7.

Rule:
• i++ → use current value, THEN increment (Post: print first, add later)
• ++i → increment FIRST, THEN use new value (Pre: add first, print later)

🐛 Common Bug: Using i++ instead of ++i inside expressions leads to logic errors.
💡 Best practice: Keep increment statements on their own line to avoid confusion.

&& (AND): If LEFT side is FALSE → skip right side entirely
|| (OR):  If LEFT side is TRUE  → skip right side entirely

In the example:
• If user == null: short-circuits → user.isActive() is NEVER called
• Without null check: NullPointerException! Most common Java runtime error.

Why it matters:
1. Safety: prevents NullPointerException
2. Performance: skips expensive operations (DB query, API call) when not needed

💡 Rule: Always put the cheaper/safer check on the LEFT side of &&

Banking example:
if (account != null && account.getBalance() >= withdrawAmount && !account.isFrozen()) {
    processWithdrawal();
}

Output:
false  ← a == b: different objects in heap (new creates new object)
true   ← a.equals(b): same characters
true   ← c == d: SAME object (String Pool/Interning! literals share reference)
true   ← c.equals(d): same characters

Why c == d is true:
String literals go into the String Pool. "RoboBank" is created once; c and d point to the SAME pooled object.

🐛 Bug in 99% of beginner Java code:
if (userInput == "yes") { ... }  // WRONG! May be false even if content matches

✅ Fix:
if ("yes".equals(userInput)) { ... }  // Note: literal.equals(var) avoids NPE if var is null
